We continue to cede the future to the Chinese, which is utterly frustrating.

I’m a dedicated “petroleum head”, owning a number of high performance autos and motorcycles, all German or Italian; I decided at my last purchase seven years ago that my next car would be electric.

About a year ago, I began to look in earnest at the used EV market, where you can absolutely steal low mileage EVs.

I have an app that aggregates ads for these cars for sale nationwide.

Every once in a while (literally, once or twice monthly), I’d get notification that a car I had saved had sold.

Things were pretty slow, so I just kind of watched.

At the beginning of our conflict with Iran, I began to notice a spike in sales to a few sold daily(!), so, I sold my 99 Porsche 911 C4 and purchased a Polestar 2, performance pack dual motor.

It is, hands down, the best car I’ve ever owned.

Ever.

Pretty, solidly built, full of cool tech and as fast as an Italian sport bike.

Disappointingly, as mentioned in the article, Polestar may no longer sell cars in the American Market, so I’m trying to figure out if I need to pivot and sell while it still has good trade in value, or to risk it and drive until the wheels fall off.

Thing is, two of the other choices I was considering were the Cadillac Lyric and the Ford Mustang Mach E.

Both are fantastic cars, as well; maybe that’s the pivot.

The current administration is so hostile to anything good and forward looking that it’s creating the US as global pariah.

comments.name: Patrick
comments.body:
The conservative court likes to use “originalism” as a sword to strike down anything progressive that they dislike, and a shield to protect any conservative policies they adore. If the Constitution is an immovable rock and we should look to it for all answers forever, then how come our founders included Article V (amendment)? How come Jefferson proclaimed that the constitution should change with the times? The founding fathers knew enough to know they didn’t have all the answers. They left it to future generations to improve and change it as society changed. They couldn’t even figure out how to deal with Slavery, which led to a massive Civil War 80 years later. Let’s drop the “originalism” and call it what it is - a conservative court helping out a conservative presidency and holding the rest of us hostage. 
The main flaw of the constitution - the bar to amend is too high. Article V has such a gigantic threshold for application that a mere 12% of the population can prevent something from passing.

comments.name: Joe Pearce
comments.body: The two situations are not at all comparable. The first, basically a law to monitor or punish moral behavior, fell afoul of a great many changes in laws, temperaments, state vs federal rights or prerogatives, etc. It is almost laughable what ensued, and SCOTUS recognized that unanimously. The second situation is no such thing. The right to bear arms was much needed, if only in order to hunt game for the kitchen table, but also to be armed and ready if (at that time) the British decided to return or there were other threats from without, but also to defend the citizens' rights to battle internal takeovers and dictatorships from within. In certain parts of the country, that first right - the hunting of game - is still relevant, and, as has been seen many times in the past decade, it may also be required to protect yourself and your family from rioters, marauders, death squads, etc. that roam the streets unimpeded by law enforcement due to political considerations. The AK47 is just a better weapon that was available in 1787, but to call it the weapon of choice for mass murderers indicates an abysmal bias o0n the writer's part.. Yes, there have been - how many? - a handful of such mass murders, some of which used an AK47, but thousands, if not perhaps millions of citizens in this country own that very weapon and do not use it for mass murder! So, do we take them away from their owners before or after we disarm the police and then the lower echelon of the military? Just asking.

The hero's  journey, the challenges of nature, the glories and flaws of human beings, the impulse for revenge, the importance of resourcefulness and the  goal of going home. So perfect to be reminded of the power of art to help us understand who we are through all time- thank you Mr. Nolan and team .

comments.name: Hudson Valley
comments.body:
I think you drove too far north. 
In MY Hudson Valley (Rockland County — also, the NY 17th Congressional District), we are fighting. Fighting for democracy, fighting for land, fighting for rights…it’s a daily fight and we are fed up.
We have lived here for almost 40 years. My husband was raised here, and we settled here when his parents moved to Florida. In the early 2000s, I taught in the Ramapo School District and witnessed the slow demolition of the school board and extra-curricular activities for children into what is now a district that heavily favors busing for Hasidic children to their schools. Our neighborhood is being converted to LLCs purchased by Brooklyn owners who in turn rent to low-income lessees with little interest in maintaining peace. Homeowners who want to sell are being stymied by Hasidim who refuse to pay their asking prices and are driving prices down. Meanwhile, our Congressman, Mike Lawler, professes to be fighting for our rights in Washington, but is actually holding meetings with “special interests” and paving the way for more low-income building, more child care facilities and schools that will only be used by Hasidim, and nothing is done. If any of us cry foul, we are immediately accused of anti-semitism, which is funny, because my husband is Jewish. We are being forced out at bottom-dollar prices with no governmental oversight or intervention. 
We are not rich. We are senior citizens who just want to survive. And we are furious.

America is doomed . We did it to ourselves and history will not be kind to us.
What will your grandchildren say about us ?

Can we just admit that there is a feudal system of billionaire overlords who suck up to whomever is in power versus regular serfs with no health care who can’t afford a home?  The ego of this country is astounding: we need to admit we’ve hit bottom before we can fix it.

In the end the helicopters on the embassy in Vietnam fleeing the on coming North Vietnamese should be burned into our memory. Might doesn’t always make things right. It was a mistake to start this war and a bigger mistake to keep trying to impose our will on one of the oldest civilizations in the world. Accept that this is a mistake and cut your losses. You can’t bomb your way out of the boxed canyon you’re in. Twelve million people showing up the leader you assassinated should have you in a state of shock.

Trump has decided to go it alone with the blessings of Republicans in Congress.   The "war" was instigated by Bibi and  Trump saw it as a way to show he had the power to act alone.  He wanted a diversion from the Epstein debacle.  It has since morphed into a standoff about the Strait. There is no comparison and  we have to stop presenting Trump's behavior in this light.

"Climate change is creating conditions that are increasingly favourable for wildfires, including hotter temperatures. Wildfire smoke can travel long distances, impacting air quality and increasing health risks for populations far removed from the original wildfire.

Wildfire smoke is a dangerous mixture of gases, fine particles and chemicals. The primary health concern is fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅). These particles can easily bypass the body’s defences, penetrate deep into the lungs and may enter the bloodstream, contributing to inflammation and systemic health effects.

Other harmful components in wildfire smoke include carbon monoxide, ozone, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide. Additionally, the convergence of air pollution, wildfire smoke and extreme heat represents a growing global health threat, with compounding effects that increase acute illness, worsen chronic diseases and contribute to preventable deaths."

I believe something was missed in the response to the recent widow.  Depression certainly is part of it. But, I have seen older people make an indirect but desperate bid to be taken care of by their children.  They don't want to ask, they want it to be offered. Appearing to be unable to care properly for themselves is a way to indirectly make the adult child aware of this need/desire.  Yes, it is manipulative to pursue it this way, but even the best of us are not at our best when we're panicked.

Perhaps she just wants to be moved closer to where the daughter lives.  Perhaps she wants to move in with the daughter.  (or maybe I'm wrong in this particular case)  The possibility of these scenarios and others is strong and the daughter should probably find a way to discuss them, even if they are not on offer.  

Asking how she is doing, as suggested, would be a good springboard into this discussion.  "Are you wanting to make some big changes?" is a non-committal way to try to tease out what the parent might have in mind.  

Chances are, eventually, the parent will need/want to live close by an adult child.

Trump’s bargaining position is worse than the one the United States had during the JCPOA negotiations. Obama did not have to deal with those issues.

So Iran has every reason to demand a deal more favorable to it than the JCPOA. And frankly, if the deal is not better for Iran than the JCPOA was, Iran should probably fire whoever negotiated it.

Or, in other words, the likely resolution of this is that the United States spends billions of dollars, depletes critical munitions, exposes its vulnerability to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, and ends up with a deal worse than the JCPOA. That is not an outcome Trump is ever going to want to own.

What could have been done differently? Probably limiting military engagement to suppressing overt development of a nuclear weapon while locating and tracking the stockpiles, and only then—if at all—launching broader military action to eliminate them. 

Eliminating the stockpiles, to a degree sufficient to cripple further nuclear development, would at least have supplied a reasonable and defined objective for starting and ending the war. But that is not what happened.

Dismal reality:

Microscopic size: a single Cyclospora parasite (called an oocyst) is only 8 to 10 micrometers in diameter.

Visual comparison:  this parasite is so small that you could fit roughly 10,000 of them on the head of a single pin.

Special laboratory detection: Doctors and food safety scientists cannot even see them using a standard office microscope unless they use a special chemical staining technique (called acid-fast staining) or look at them under ultraviolet (UV) light, which causes the parasite to naturally glow or fluoresce.

Because we cannot inspect food to see if it is infected, following regional recalls and cooking food thoroughly are our only reliable protections.

One of the most useful points in this interview is where the distinction is made between capitalism and markets.  They are not synonyms.  I think that point needs to be made more and more.  

Capitalism is not a meritocracy where profits are distributed equitably.  In an extreme example, take Bezos.  Yes, he hatched the idea of Amazon and should be rewarded for such.  However, his reward FAR outweighs his contribution to it.  At some point in the past, the growth of Amazon became primarily the product of its employees at all levels, not Bezos.   But because he owns so much of it, Bezos reaps rewards far beyond his scope of usefulness.  

This is the very definition of an unjust system.  Amazon can continue to grow and exist in a more just system.  All that needs to change is the distribution of the rewards.

This column shows why we need The Ethicist to put us in touch with our better angels.

Especially readers of the New York Times and those who comment on its articles.  I have never seen such unforgiving, shortsighted attitudes, at least not since last week's Social Q's.  The general tenor is, "You're bad, bad, bad!  The heck with you."

We don't really know from this description, but, as Appiah recognizes, LW seems to think that there could be some mileage in her children seeing their father.  She wouldn't write this if she thought that the father would make it impossible.  Commenters cite "abuse," but what LW writes is "verbally abusive," and I wonder what that means.  I think that LW is trying to be kind both to the father and to her children, because it could be meaningful to all of them to have this contact.  

I don't mean to dismiss the feelings and experiences of commenters who have cut off abusive parents, but maybe this situation is importantly different from theirs.

I do think that can be a parent's role to counsel their children to look beyond what they currently see, to things that are truly important.

comments.name: Janice
comments.body:
Mr. Appiah's responses to questions like this often frustrate me. I sometimes wonder whether he consults with therapists or family counselors before giving this kind of advice. It sounds like the mother has already encouraged her children to visit their father. At this point, she needs to let it go and allow them to decide for themselves.

As someone who has no contact with an abusive family member and has often been told to reconcile so I won't feel guilty later, I can unequivocally say I would have no guilt should they pass. Not every estranged relationship can or should be repaired.

Mr. Appiah says it would be kind to visit an abusive parent. But what about kindness to yourself by refusing to be abused again? Protecting yourself isn't cruel—it's healthy, appropriate and loving. People don't change just because time passes. They change only if they acknowledge the harm they've caused, take responsibility, and do the work to change. Until then, no one should feel obligated to put themselves back in harm's way.

Let's be honest: the person who would likely feel the most relief if the estranged children visited their father is their mother. She wants it to happen because it would ease her own mind, but that doesn't mean it's what's best for her children. Mom, your kids are adults. Trust that they know what's best for them, even if it makes you feel uncomfortable.

From their taking (sometimes torturing) our embassy hostages from '79 to '81, through massacres of Jews in Argentina and Marines in Lebanon, to constant harassment of Israel, to the state of play today, asserting they should control the Strait -- how many more deaths and insults to the international order are we willing to allow?
Lord knows Trump and Hegseth are the last duo you'd want to carry out this mission (thank you, the 77m Trump voters), but that's who we have. And using force without one hand tied behind our back (the modus vivendi of Vietnam through Afghanistan) will achieve at a minimum the free opening of the Strait. I would argue a real regime change would make the next half-century in the Mideast better than the past. 
Israel will have to be controlled, too, of course, especially given their abuses in the West Bank and Gaza. But for the sake of the region, the safety of American allies and interests, and any woman who doesn't want to wear scarves on her head, the mullahs should fall.

comments.name: Daniel Kaiserski

The manly powdered wig and tights gave way to the blazer and tie. 

Many years before, the manly Roman toga gave way to effeminate pants. 

O tempora, o mores.

comments.name: James Vohr
comments.body: The decline of men wearing hats correlates with the ascendance of the idea of toxic masculinity.  Men emasculated by the feminist movement wear boys' hats today.  Without hat checks, what is one even to do with a baseball hat in a restaurant?  It doesn't go on the table, and nobody wants to put it on the floor, so they are worn.  The wearing of baseball hats is just one symptom of the overall decline in dress.  My father went to work every day in a shirt with a tie and a jacket.  How many men show up at the workplace in coat and tie today?  The clothes make the man, as they say, and the loss of formality in wear mirrors the loss or formality overall which translates to a loss in manners and a loss in respect.

comments.name: Tom Gelsthorpe
comments.body:
I have two fedoras: one of brown fur felt for the cold part of the year,; the other a genuine Panama in a fedora shape for warm weather.  I wear one or the other for any sort of urban foray.  Less formal hats serve for boating, country walks, etc.

I get more polite treatment from everyone, young or old, man or woman, when wearing the fedora shape.  I can recommend them for that reason alone.  For a bonus they keep the sun off your nose and ears, and your hair tidy but not matted, without being too cumbersome.

I'm confident they will regain popularity -- maybe in my lifetime.  The pendulum on goofy attire in public has swung too far for too long.

The Fedora is—was—a tidy, classy look. At a baseball game. Walking downtown, heading to lunch. And removed upon arrival.

This was well done! I also hate it when people press up against me in line, or don't let people in earlier rows in an airplane disembark first. We are all going to the same place and unless you really have a very tight connection, don't do this. It is just rude.

We also have a queueing gene in Canada and people get very offended about skipping, or at least they used to. I think sometimes people bring habits from other places that break this to some extent. I live in fear of when my Italian partner gets impatient with a line - anywhere - as being able to skip a line is almost a point of pride. On the other side, I often find that if I am not assertive in Italy someone will skip ahead of me, too, even if it is blatantly obvious that I was there first. In Canada, my partner marvels at how people even line up to get on the bus. Someone gave him bus fare one time when he didn't have the correct change and he still tells that story with wonder!

In some post offices there is a system whereby people ask when they arrive who was the person that arrived immediately before them (the last in line) and that is how they know when it it their turn.

E 4/4 confers a 10 fold increased risk, and I do have signs on MRI and amyloid scans. This knowledge allowed me to be a research subject, and to enroll in a specialty clinic. 

True, there is no current effective treatment, but I can control my lifestyle. I would have never given up my one drink a day without this knowledge, and I take things like low dose lithium, fish oil, and other supplements. (Disclaimer that this is research stuff only at this point.)

Yes, I'm afraid. But I can plan for the future, financially and otherwise.

comments.body:
The situation discussed in this column emphasizes the importance of having conversations about what happens after one spouse dies long before one is sick.
Obviously, such conversations are likely more appropriate and understood to be needed when people are older. Nonetheless everyone should be doing advance care planning and preparation because you never know when serious illness or death will occur.

comments.name: Megom
comments.body: As always, Dr. Gottleib provides exceptional insights. But I'm surprised she didn't suggest connecting with hospice care. Hospice care professionals are extraordinary and in addition to providing meaningful end of life care, can facilitate these painful conversations.

comments.name: Veery
comments.body: I wish I had the courage and insight to take on this conversation 6 years ago. We were both in denial as to the outcome of his cancer. As it is, the grief and guilt are still with me.

comments.name: Late Boomer
comments.body: We all could benefit from such conversations, and not when one partner is terminal. Both my late mother and I had partners who died most unexpectedly. As in ... my father woke up one Sunday morning, walked to the bathroom, and dropped dead. I wish I'd had the "luxury" of having more late-life conversations with him. My partner died of internal bleeding after Christmas dinner. I still haven't found a few things he stashed away.

comments.name: Eloise
comments.body: Thank you for this great article and all the comments are so helpful. (Enjoy every sandwich).

comments.name: Ann
comments.body: I cared for my husband for three years while he was dying of Alzheimer’s.  I will not address the emotions. Others have done that.  I will address practical matters.  When my husband was diagnosed, we realized we had to address the financial ramifications.  Since I could get hit by a car, we acted for both of us.  All the powers of attorney were settled, including making our daughter responsible if one of us died. We had meetings with our financial person and lawyer.  We added a codicil setting out our wishes for our remains.  As my husband became sicker I took over all the finances.  Dealing with this stuff after death is hard enough.  My knowledge of our finances made a tough situation bearable. And, my condolences.  This is a rough road.

comments.name: Seer
comments.body: My husband didn’t want to talk about it when he was dying. His willpower to stay alive was fierce. Despite having cancer for three years, doctors didn’t say outright it was terminal until a few months before he died, which made me bringing up the topic fraught. This also meant we didn’t have financial discussions about what would happen to me after, beyond him vaguely asking friends and family to look after me when he was gone while he was dying. All of our focus was on the immense effort to keep him alive. A year or two out, and I am still dealing with the ramifications.

comments.name: Professor
comments.body:
I have stage IV cancer. It's uncurable and will kill me, but I don't know when. There are treatments that haven't been tried yet, but the ones I have had fail fester and faster. 

My wife and I talk about it incessantly. Maybe too much. But the children are young and her finances without me will be strained but not impossible. We talk about the children's needs as they grow older; she asks me about that because she was never a boy and didn't grow up in the U.S. We discuss budgeting to make savings last, which hopefully with her lower income, will stretch until kids are independent. If she can get a better job, so much the better, but it's hard now. We talk about spending money to create whole-family memories, too. We've gone on trips and to events. 

At first it was me who took the initiative to talk about these things. She engaged reluctantly in a "maybe you'll get better" kind of way. Her denial used to irritate me. Now that she's joined me in facing the inevitable, I miss it.  We still hope for more time. So the boys will be older when I pass. So we have more time together. So we can create more memories. So we can build more savings from my income. So new treatments can be developed to prolong...  prolong... prolong.

comments.name: Ethan Mitchell
comments.body: Stereotypes of nationalities do have some truth to them, but they, of course, do not apply to all people from that country.  Argentinians do consider themselves superior and there's an inherent arrogance and racism associated with that, which is reflected in many of the players and fans.  It's obnoxious, but I know quite a few Argentinians personally and I consider them great people.  Sports reflects a natural tendency of humans to be tribal -- it's ok when it just leads to spirited competition; it is not ok when it leads to racism and disrespect.  Argentinians and people of other countries in Latin America, most notably Chileans, have a certain hostility toward one another.  Same for the Portuguese and Spanish.  Same for the English and French, although they both agree that they dislike the Germans more.  And the Swedes look down on the Norwegians and Finns.  Australians and New Zealanders.  New Yorkers and Bostonians.  Northern Italians and Southern Italians.  Scotland and Ireland versus England.  As long as it doesn't get ugly or violent or truly disrespectful, it's probably fine and just the way of things, but it's a slippery slope to racism, discrimination, and even war.

The only time they ever banded together was to fight off outsiders in this case the Russians. It’s what the show ‘Game of Thrones’ was based and written. There was a period of a 100 year war where 20 million people were killed, basically half the population of Europe at the time. comments.name: Thom Wright
comments.body:
A couple decades ago, in a legal fight (I was the plaintiff) against the US government which stole well over $100K of my equipment, my lawyer and I met with the Judge and the governments two lawyers pre-trial.  After the judge dismissed the two government lawyers to go discuss G's active violations of law, my lawyer and I sat there chatting with the judge.  

I explained the attempts by a federal prosecutor and federal investigators to extort perjury.  The prosecutor made it quite clear, unless I committed perjury under oath to support his prosecution, his two investigators would commit perjury under oath testifying I admitted to being a part of a conspiracy.  I was merely the builder, constructing a house for the defendants in that case.  

I asked the judge why.  His simple answer, "incompetence."  I suspect that is the real issue in all of these.  Government bureaucrats are far too incompetent to successfully pursue their jobs so, they cheat.

comments.name: Rick Shaw
comments.body: Back in the 90s/00s, I was a public company CEO twice for businesses that I built and took public.  Twice, the SEC looked for insider trading because of stock movements.  They had me deliver 10 years of records.  Their policy was to never close an investigation, just let it linger.   There was no insider trading, but years later, we still had no resolution.  In a different company in which I was an investor, the FDA went after the business in the hopes of extracting a material settlement.  After a year-long investigation, we had absolute documentation of our correctness, including a legal opinion that pre-dated their investigation.  They then told us that we either had to pay a $5M fine or they would pursue a criminal investigation against the lab head.  We settled under threat.  Finally, we had another education business where the FTC investigated an advertising claim.  It became clear they were after big game.  We were a small company with no violations.  They proposed, and we accepted, a $13M settlement, then permanently suspended the fine - in other words, no fine.  This was done to "save face" and to let them go after bigger fish.  We had to live with a public "fine" when we sold the business.  Time and time again, gov abuse of power has been my experience.  It is hardly a surprise that I am skeptical of giving more power to the government.

In the excessive hubris of the Peak Woke era, progressive censors at Twitter were confident that they could control the discourse by simply banning everyone who said something that offended them (a very long list, given the extensive ideological commitments of the censors).  The ferocious backlash to progressive ideological management of public discourse, highlighted above all by Musk's purchase of Twitter, is an indispensable precondition for Trump's 2024 victory.   Lacking the effective ability to silence and censor right-wing perspectives, which the Left relied upon and took for granted for so many years, made it very difficult for the Left to respond to right-wing attacks, or even to realize initially how deeply unpopular many Left-wing views are with the public.

The Bx12 Select Bus Service on Fordham Road is a textbook case of infrastructure that fails to deliver. Dedicated lanes are already in place, yet the route remains among the slowest in the Bronx—strangled by routine violations, weak enforcement, and mixed traffic that treats bus priority as optional. Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s push to secure these lanes and keep them open is the correct first step. But lane enforcement alone will not solve the deeper connectivity crisis facing Bronx riders.

What requires priority attention is direct, reliable bus access from the Bronx to LaGuardia Airport. The current lack of streamlined service forces unnecessary transfers that waste time and erode reliability for airport workers, travelers, and connecting passengers. A ride on the BxM7 makes the operational case clear: a limited-stop bus serving the Hunts Point vicinity is feasible and would tap into real demand patterns without requiring entirely new infrastructure.

The improvements to the Bruckner Expressway present a strategic opening to expand both local and express bus service. By integrating strong bus priority into those upgrades and establishing new direct links from the 96th Street and Second Avenue corridor in Manhattan (Q train station) into the Bronx, we can finally deliver faster, more dependable connections where they are needed most—serving working communities and critical economic hubs without compromise.

After the exodus of largely middle class African-Americans, the city became such a godforsaken backwater that in the 1950s, when I-95 was built, it completely sidestepped Wilmington. Regardless of their animus toward Black people, how could the white powers that be allow this to happen? I learned a couple of years ago when I spent some time as a tour guide in Wilmington. For such a small city, you see, Wilmington has a very large historic district of lovely homes —and when all is said and done, home is everything. So white middle and upper-class Wilmington lived their lives, unjudged in these nice homes – – some of which were looted from fleeing Black people. And to this day, the massacre and coup are not widely discussed, certainly not to the degree that chattel slavery and Jim Crow are formally addressed by Wilmington’s coastal sisters, Charleston and Savannah.

So - the article outlines and stresses the Argentinian focus and resolute towards righting a wrong (the Falkland Islands) - to a point that its engrained at their U18 training facility.  To the degree that national pride is at stake based on the match’s outcome.  

Pundits are forecasting a very physical and emotionally draining game - for both sides, which will potentially result in multiple yellow and maybe red cards.  As with all matches - the game play will result in either a very close game with extra time (30 minutes) and a shootout to determine the victor or a comfortable margin of victory (such as yesterday’s semi (Spain v France).  The former will result in the victor being not only overly fatigued due to the extra playing time - which will be compounded by one less day of recovery time - but also the potential of players either being barred from the Championship game due to a red card or their play limited due to carrying a yellow card into the match.  Alternatively, if it is a one-sided game, I could envision the losing side team taking runs at their opponents to cause injury.

In both cases, the ultimate victor of today’s match-up will be Spain.

The focus on Bay Ridge is interesting. Unlike Bensonhurst, Borough Park, Flatbush, and the like that produced the overwhelming majority of famous folks, Bay Ridge was known for few things. Most importantly it was the home of the Penthouse-Pastels long running Disco-Nightclub often compared to the Copacabana, which was the actual spot the producers wanted to film Saturday Night Fever. in 1994, several members of our theatre group took a 5day package trip to Iceland.  Airfare, hotel and breakfast included.  After checking in at the hotel my friend and i went wandering around the city while the rest of them napped.  We
saw posters for The Volcano Show and went to buy tickets for that evening. The cinematographer, whose films were the show, discounted our fee because we were "in the arts" (i think his name was peterson) and that night gave us a 3hour show in what was basically his garage.  We drove outside the city Route 30, i can never forget, and were rescued from a snow bank by a family driving across the ice fields. Buffet dinner at the hotel was really delicious.  We only ate "out" one night at a restaurant called "Argentine" where i had one of the best steak dinners of my life. Everyone was amazingly kind, i.e. I dropped my camera in the blue lagoon and the receptionist in our hotel called her boyfriend who was hiking, and for permission go to his camera shop which was closed for the weekend, to let me buy several disposable cameras.  We saw and petted Iceland horses in a field (so sweet) drove out to Borganis which was basically empty but the hotel restaurant served us a lovely meal anyway; we had icecream at the Pearl.  We did the Friday visit to the cafes and went to one jazz club to drink aquavit. It was one of the best times of my life.  I would love to visit again, though it probably won't be as personally friendly and charming..

comments.name: Tommy Boy
comments.body: The deadly sharpshooter strikes again. I remember when Napa in 1994 and 2000 destroyed over 1,000 acres of Northern California vineyards and caused roughly $30 million in damages. Then there was the phyloxera disease infection throughout the vineyards.  It affected up 80% of the valley’s vineyards, leading to a massive, multi-million-dollar replanting effort using highly resistant rootstocks throughout the 1990s. Just what the wineries need with sales figures down over 20% or more and wine tastings down over 50%.

comments.name: JC Schultz
comments.body: This serious insect pest carrying Pierce's disease cannot be controlled by usual means because it moves around and lives and breeds in natural areas that cannot be cleared because of environmental laws. Control must focus on the Pierce's disease microbe more than the insect. UC Davis is producing resistant vines, but they take a long time to establish during which there is no production. Meanwhile nurseries are obligated to ensure that vines they sell do not carry the insect. Apparently that failed in this case. This problem will grow worse with climate change, since the insect normally prefers warm, humid climates.

comments.body: New York once allowed elephants and other wild animals to be marched through the Midtown Tunnel and into Manhattan to perform at Madison Square Garden. Families brought their children to watch and cheer, unable—or unwilling—to see the misery behind the spectacle. Legality and tradition did not make that practice humane. The same is true here. New York should lead on animal welfare, not be forced into doing the right thing only after another collapse, another runaway horse or another death. It has been long enough.

comments.name: Tim
comments.body:
There are plenty of electric horseless carriages in use in other cities. Sorry if it looks like a promotion, but here's a website for Antwerp and Brussels, Belgium. I saw one of them in person in March, 2026, and it seemed spacious, comfortable, and 100% silent.

https://www.e-carriagetour.com/en/

Here's a NY Times report on the product:

https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/19/world/europe/horse-drawn-carriage-brussels.html?smid=url-share

Why would anyone want to go back to the days when tons of horse waste had to be removed from NYC's streets every day? And the time (until, maybe 1990) when the drivers were Irish immigrants who had been around horses most of their lives are long gone. If the number of driver jobs declines, that's because the businesses refuse to take out loans to buy electric carriages. The only jobs lost will be shoveling out the horse stalls.

Another note: One reason the paved roads in the southeast corner of Central Park are so crowded and chaotic are the number of lifetime-free-parking spaces for Parks Department (and Conservancy) employees and contractors, as well as other city employees. There are too many cars and trucks on these "pedestrian" roads.

The revived Stockton Market, the Starving Artist cafe across the street (which features live music now and then), and the soon-to-open Terra Mare restaurant on Bridge Street are all welcome additions. Not mentioned in the article is the Stockton Food Store, a deli in the old Pennsylvania Railroad station next to the Shell station on Bridge Street. 1. It's an easy drive to Hopewell, NJ, with its own unique historic homes, great restaurants, and shopping. 
2. Speaking of Hopewell, when the Lindbergh baby kidnapping happened in 1932, very little lodging was available for journalists and many stayed at the Stockton Inn.

comments.name: Chris
comments.body: Thank you for a wonderful article highlighting our friends who proudly run small businesses in Stockton, New Jersey. Since 1915 the anchor business of Stockton has been Hendricks Appliances, a remarkable family run store that has somehow been overlooked. Stockton is not Stockton without Hendricks, arguably the heart of the town...

comments.name: Lawrence
comments.body: Grew up in the area and have the happiest memories of floating down the river in inner tubes, getting soft-serve at Dilly’s, and biking along the canal under the mottled light of the massive sycamores that predate the Revolutionary War. While I live in California now, it’s been wonderful to back and visit recently and see how a new generation has invested in sweet little Stockton, the best-kept secret between NY and Philly. The old Victorian houses have been lovingly restored and painted, people are bustling about in town, and there’s still the warmth and spirit unique to the tiny river towns— I can think of few places where hay farmers, antique dealers, East Village elder statesman gays, young families, and historical reenactors are all waiting in line for coffee together. A very special place!

comments.name: Former Hunterdon Resident
comments.body: I lived in Raritan Township, on the Flemington border and had been coming to the River Towns area most of my life.  Charming little Stockton fell on some hard times and it is great to see it revived.  I remember the old Stockton Inn.  Despite the risk of flooding, the area, including Lambertville has a rural/river charm that is unique.  However, the risk is that the same "Hamptonization" that occurred in New Hope, PA will creep to the NJ side of the river.  What once was a charming artist colony with unique and quirky restaurants has become an overpriced tourist destination that retains little of its original appeal.  I left the pseudo-Manhattan vide there and returned to Northern NJ where I have easy access to the real thing.

comments.name: GT
comments.body:
We being in the club of "second home" people across the river in PA (small village a few miles north) wish to give a shout out to Stockton and all that is happening.  The rebuilt Stockton Inn is fantastic and we love all that has happened at Woolverton, especially at the Northridge restaurant on Sunday night when they do a simple menu. BYOB as well. The farmers market / tea shop  ... my wine shop. Miss getting my car fixed but I can drink beer at the old shop.  How many towns have an appliance store!  Gas station saves me from pumping my own gas. Thank you!

Floods in the early 00's and the lingering effects of the 08 economic downturn hung like a dark cloud over all the Delaware river towns  ... Covid hit just as things were starting to really move again. Thankfully people stuck with it and we have the rebuilt Stockton Inn and Woolverton and the other shops that make the little town special.  Too bad nothing seems to be happening across the bridge at Centerbridge.  

Old historic properties are not for everyone ...  if they are the area can't be matched for it's unique character and beauty. So much is going on in the area.

comments.name: That said
comments.body: Well, "Anonymous" well noted, could well (well, well, well) give a listen to Bruce Springsteen's "My Hometown" as a tribute, in part, to downtrodden towns like the Stockton "he" so grievously had to bear as a teacher back in the day.  Indeed, he has a case.  But then, again, another listen to Springsteen's "Glory Days" when decades ago, Stockton was on the map because of an article (NOT an advertisement but an article) published in the New York Times extolling the unique treasure located there, Schuck's Garage, where Richard Schuck maintained the finest German car repair shop in the New York City area.

comments.name: Dave
comments.body:
I'm a Duwamish tribal member. I served on our Tribal Council in 2024.

Recognition is a real injustice, and the Chinook are on the right path. Nothing I say here takes away from that.

But the Duwamish story has a second half this piece misses. The nonprofit that holds our money and runs on Real Rent donations, Duwamish Tribal Services, operates with almost no oversight from its own members. I know because I sat on the council and asked for basic financial records I was entitled to, and never got them. The rest is in the public IRS filings: millions held in cash, legal spending that dwarfs what reaches members, and a board and council made up of the same few people.

When other tribes question the Duwamish, it's easy to read it as rivalry over money. Most of it is about something else. The author of this article should follow up on some details before throwing the Muckleshoot tribe under the bus.

I've documented all of it, sourced to the public filings, for anyone who wants the details.

These small bands of often mixed-race people demanding tribal recognition often do not have any tribal structure, subsistence knowledge, shared language, lands, artifacts, kinship stories, or even a shared culture.

They are not recognized as tribes because they are not tribes.

Many of them are rank opportunists.  They want casinos.  They want to sell booze and cigarettes without regulation or taxes.  They want natural resources (in Washington, recognized tribes with treaty rights get half of all the fish and other resources).

Please, stop with the sympathy for cultural appropriators.  Real tribes are deserving of our support and recognition, and they need to be protected from these folks.

This isn’t just happening in California, it’s happening all over the country. This happened to my husband. He was born in the reservation. This is a key way that the federal government keeps tribes fighting against each other. The funding never increases; instead, for all federally recognized tribes the money decreases. comments.name: Dan Hewson
comments.body: In the picture of him in the Mets uniform at 82, he looked like he probably still had some pitches left that would have bedazzled today's batters. Hope he got a large settlement in his age discrimination suit.

comments.name: Barry
comments.body: Sometimes when I recall an old ballplayer a specific statistic of theirs comes to mind. When I hear Phil Regan’s name 14 and 1 automatically pops up. He was a great one, and they didn’t call him the Vulture for nothing. RIP Phil. You were a big part of those great Dodger teams of the 60’s.

comments.name: ped
comments.body:
I attended that game at Dodger Stadium in '66 when Koufax pitched 11 innings and Regan relieved in the 12th.  Jim Bunning pitched for the Phillies and also went 11 innings.  One of my best and most indelible memories.  I wonder when was the last time a starter lasted 11 innings.  

Thanks for the memories, Mssrs. Koufax, Bunning and Regan.

comments.name: American exile
comments.body: I recall attending a Cubs game in the summer of 1969 at Wrigley Field -- Regan was relief pitching, with a unique, semi-underhand movement, keeping the ball out of sight almost until he released it. The plate umpire stopped play several times to examine the ball for 'foreign substances" and at one point actually frisked Regan, who cooperated, albeit with a sly grin. The game went on -- I don't recall the outcome, except that Phil Regan made that umpire look like an idiot.

comments.name: Times Reader 1978
comments.body: Following the Tigers in the early '60s, I was sorry to see Regan seemingly lose it in '64 and '65 after having a few good seasons at the start of his career.  The team lost faith in him, then the Dodgers got him and turned him into a really good closer. Always sorry the Tigers didn't figure out he wasn't a starter.

comments.name: saulfeggio
comments.body:
The baseball glove that I saved and saved for as a 13-year-old was a Phil Regan model. 
I played off and on in leagues for more than 30 years using that glove. I re-stitched the webbing myself several times. IT served me well. 
When Phil Regan was the pitching coach of the team I follow I arranged to meet him and he autographed it for me. 
I still have that glove, nearly 60 years on.
When I go, it goes with me.

“ When I moved here in the ’90s, to be a soccer fan was to be an outsider,” he said. “It was a hardy bunch of lifers holding on to one another for dear life. This World Cup will erode that forever, and to be a soccer fan will be as normal as being an N.F.L. fan.”

Sadly, he is wrong. 

When this World Cup is over, the novelty will wear off for many and the NFL is soon to begin again.

MLS games are easy to ignore if you don’t have AppleTV, for instance.

Mainstream media (whatever that is) coverage is still difficult to find and fragmented streaming of different competitions means following all major club and country competitions is expensive.

I’m a huge football/soccer/futbol fan, but realistically, soccer will return to the sporting margins in the U.S. and Canada after all the hype.

In communist China, the government is so fragile and scared of its own people, they have to ban ideas that threaten their rule. Laughable.

comments.name: Sam Chittum
comments.body:
Same playbook, different country. This time around the snake oil salesmen are billionaires with their hands out peddling environmentally rapacious infrastructure in the form of water guzzling, heat generating, ecosystem destroying hyper-scale data centers. Without any input from the people who live next door to these monstrosities. 

If having a hyperscale data center as a neighbor is so great, why are deals to build these mega projects being done behind closed doors with little or no public input?

Massive data centers use up to 5 million gallons of water a day or as much as a midsized city of 50,000. The water is used to cool thousands of heat generating servers that run 24-7 generating a nonstop 90 decibel hum that is so loud it travels for miles and penetrates the walls of homes and schools. (A data center plan here in the desert in the Coachella Valley wanted to build adjacent to an elementary school for 680 children.)

They create heat islands that raise temperatures anywhere from 5 to  15 degrees. If you live in the desert as I do, where temperatures routinely rise to 110 degrees in the summer, that’s simply unlivable. 

Furious local protests here beat back a similar proposal for a hyperscale data center next to the city of Coachella that last year received less than two inches of rain and depends on an aquifer that requires 80 percent recharge from the dying Colorado River. 

Because you can’t drink data.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body:
AI sovereignty is now a key factor in national defense. 

India is well behind and cannot develop it's own frontier models but they can work with Chinese open source models, post train to remove the Chinese propaganda and any backdoors (it is possible to train a software generating model to insert subtle security flaws into generated code) and then run in domestic data centers.

In a world where top AI models are more dangerous than nuclear weapons this is an existential issue.

comments.name: Jai
comments.body: Hey Chandrababu,build a desalination plant to address the water issue of the data center.Just do it!

comments.name: Shekhar
comments.body:
Of course, where India's oligarchs such as the Adanis and Ambanis are concerned, the Modi government bends over backwards to facilitate their projects. Google is headed by Sundar Pichai, who knows which levers to pull in India to get unpalatable projects sanctioned. The AI data centers promise to create stress in water and electricity supplies without creating substantial jobs.

And why on earth should subsidised land, water and electricity be offered by the government to such projects is beyond me.

comments.body: Chandrababu Naidu transformed Hyderabad from a dusty town into a world-class city within a decade. He has the vision and experience to pull this off.

comments.name: North County
comments.body:
AI is a global race to the bottom. Like all new technologies the cost of production (excluding energy, water and distribution) gets cheaper with every new entrant.  But the information used to build large language models is fixed even when translated to other languages.

The costs ( monetary, environmental and cultural) are significant with outcomes yet to be determined. 

I may be old but this feels to much like the 80's which to my mid boomer generation was financially tough. 

We have pulled back and are bracing for a disruptive outcome.  We cannot afford to loose what we have to live on with Congresses failure to address the SS, Health Insurance, student debt and the every day effects of inflation on food, transportation and utilities.  

We know others who are doing the dame.

comments.name: John Virgone
comments.body:
The fallout.....
My electric bill this past summer was unexplainably about 40% higher than last summer with approximately the same usage.

Each month this summer I received a notice from my utility indicating that my usage was significantly higher than the neighbors (the neighbors received the same letter) and that we should look at ways to be more efficient.

Little did we know that our added expense was in support of needed infrastructure expansion to serve the AI industry which is poised to further enrich the rich and powerful on the back of the multitudes.

As far as I am concerned the AI rage we now encounter could go away tomorrow with no detriment to society as it represents one of the most dehumanizing concepts ever devised and goes against the natural order  of the way things were meant to be.

Look for water bills to increase next.

comments.name: David
comments.body: Goddess bless Alice Oseman...and everyone involved in bringing her work off the page and into the world. The first season completely deconstructed me, and I eventually lost count of how many times I watched it. The process was tremendously healing, and I came out of it steeled against anything and anyone who falls short of full-throated support and respect for queer people--and I've been out and proud since the late 80s. I enjoyed the subsequent two seasons, and I know I will enjoy this final film, because I love these characters and their story...but it has been the existentially cathartic existence of Alice's creation (the books AND the shows) that has been transformative for me and for so many others. She has secured her place in the queer pantheon.

comments.name: John Brown Physician
comments.body:
I know physicians involved with his cancer care in NZ. 
Pneumonia is a well known complication of Cart-T therapy and bone marrow transplant. 
Immuno senescence is real after age 65. The immune system falls off exponentially. This is why over 65 year olds get flu vaccines. 
This impact is magnified by any cancer therapy. 
Sam Neil had an amazing life, and by all accounts was a dignified, honest individual. Admired by many.

comments.name: JPSci
comments.body:
I live less than a mile from the SK Hynix plant being built in that middle of a residential neighborhood in Indiana. There was strong community opposition to locating that plant here. The local zoning board changed the zoning of that site from R1 residential to heavy industrial, in a less-than-transparent action. These plants have the potential to poison air and water with PFAS and other toxic chemicals, use huge amounts of water and energy and discharge toxic waste. The residents, schools and others affected were never told why this was not being placed in an industrial area rather than in the middle of homes, schools and day care facilities. 
    I just saw the remarkable 1970s film Chinatown. The parallels to corruption and power in massive developments like this, and in the expansion of LA in the film, are unmistakable. 
    The media has shown little interest in this (but thanks for this article) and no interest in what was pushed through in Indiana. Who cares about a small city and its residents here in the Midwest, or villagers and city residents in India, or where the water is going to come from in Phoenix? These plants are toxic and guzzle resources and money. The mega billionaires run the show.

comments.name: Basta
comments.body:
In 2004 I wired money from my US account to a private bank in Buenos Aires called Banco Piano, to withdraw it as cash to buy a car.  Cash is king there. 
Amongst the stack of US 100's given to me by the bank, were 2 fake bills. I didn't know, but the car seller's bank did. No recourse with Banco Piano of course. I'd left their premises. I suspected they did it deliberately. 22 years later I am sure they did. 

The counterfeit problem is endemic in South America. 

If there's a case for Bitcoin, this is a strong one.

comments.name: Gael

Given the importance of trust and the developments in counterfeiting technology highlighted in this piece, it feels like switching materials could be a good long-term solution (assuming polymer notes as difficult to forge as they seem to be). It’s also nice to never worry about accidentally running your bills through the wash.

comments.name: MatteO
comments.body:
Fascinating article!
When I was 13, I xeroxed a dollar bill at my dad's office for fun.  I think it was more rudimentary than I realized, but I did try to endow it with some authenticity by soaking it in a solution of green food coloring and tea.

I brought it to school to show my friends at lunch and it got passed around.  One of them tried to use it.  Partway through the next period, a very serious-looking man escorted me from class and asked me to bring my things.  I had no idea that schools even *had* police officers.  Despite being a naive kid and not having taken the process of counterfeiting too seriously (it was a black-and-white copy, after all), the next two hours I and my three "co-conspirators" were questioned and threatened by officer Ritter.  Thirty-plus years later, the contempt with which he snarled the words "daddy's copier" still echoes in my mind when I think about this, and elicits the same disgust in him.  A whopping six days of suspension I received.  And I never did this again.

If I am not mistaken, estimated hundreds of millions of barrels of oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz shortly before and after the preliminary MOU was signed. That should add to the reserves around the world and help create some buffers.

In my opinion, for most of us, there is really no point in spending too much energy tracking day-to-day or hour-by-hour fluctuations in oil prices in the futures market as determined by algos, traders, and institutional investors in the absence of major catalyst events. I tend to think that those movements are largely tied to little more than changing expectations and biases based on a continuous news feed and its interpretation by those participants. I wouldn't be surprised if some market volatilities were created deliberately to make profits. In my view, it will be more interesting to observe what reasons or factors are cited to justify the price spikes and whether those same reasons and factors are equally applied to generate downward pressures later. I believe we've all witnessed this cycle play out once already.
